\begin{proof}By the definition of addition.\end{proof}

\begin{proof}By induction on $n$.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:even-sum} If $a$ and $b$ are even integers, then $a + b$ is even.\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}Since $a$ is even, $a = 2k$ for some integer $k$. Since $b$ is even, $b = 2l$ for some integer $l$. Then $a + b = 2k + 2l = 2(k + l)$, so $a + b$ is even.\end{proof}

about: The theorem is true but the proof's first step is false (n^2 is not always even). The gap must land on that step, not on the theorem.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:sq-plus} For every natural number $n$, $n^2 + n$ is even.\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}For every natural number $n$, $n^2$ is even. Also $n^2$ and $n$ have the same parity. Hence $n^2 + n$ is the sum of two even numbers, so it is even.\end{proof}

about: A false theorem with a plausible-sounding proof. Any pass is a false acceptance.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:odd-prime} Every odd natural number $n > 1$ is prime.\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}Since $n$ is odd, $2$ does not divide $n$. A number with no factor $2$ has no proper factors at all. Hence $n$ is prime.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:flt-little} Let $p$ be a prime and $a$ an integer not divisible by $p$. Then $a^{2(p-1)} \equiv 1 \pmod p$.\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}By Fermat's little theorem, $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$. Squaring both sides gives $a^{2(p-1)} \equiv 1 \pmod p$.\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:goldbach-small} Every even integer $n$ with $4 \le n \le 10^{18}$ is the sum of two primes.\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}Oliveira e Silva, Herzog and Pardi verified by computer that every even integer $n$ with $4 \le n \le 4 \cdot 10^{18}$ is the sum of two primes. Since $10^{18} \le 4 \cdot 10^{18}$, the claim follows.\end{proof}
